claim: A one-factor structure of group task scores appears in most human-group datasets: in Woolley 2010 first factor was 43.4% (40 groups) and 44.1% (152 groups); Rowe 2021 meta found 163 of 171 task correlations positive (95%) and a mean first factor of 43.03% over 19 samples.
agent_test: Run our agent on a task battery at equal tokens and check for a positive manifold; do not call it a trait unless correlations hold across scaffolds.

claim: The reported share of variance carried by the factor depends on the metric. First-factor eigenvalue share is about 43%, but average variance extracted (AVE, from standardized loadings) is about 30% across 49 loadings (Rowe) and 19.6% in the corrected Riedl 2021 (loadings 0.27 to 0.52). A 44% AVE was arithmetically implausible with loadings at most 0.52 (0.52 squared is 0.27).
agent_test: When we report any general factor for our agent, report both eigenvalue share and AVE, and never quote one as the other.

claim: Riedl 2021 correction: AVE changed from 44% to 19.6% with loadings unchanged; the 3-task Model 1 is saturated (0 df), the 5-task model fits acceptably (CFI .93, RMSEA .046) and the 8-task model fits modestly (CFI .833, RMSEA .052). Authors still claim one factor.
agent_test: Check fit of our own factor models by CFI and RMSEA and avoid saturated models.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: c has only moderate external validity: Rowe 2021 meta-analysis gives c to criterion-task r=.26 (95% CI .10 to .40, 8 samples, 857 groups, I2=86.5%); Riedl 2021 leave-one-task-out prediction r=.40 (CI .26 to .53).
agent_test: Test whether a score from n tasks predicts a held-out task for our scaffold; expect modest r.

claim: Member intelligence predicts c weakly in Woolley 2010 (mean IQ r=.15, max r=.19) and Rowe 2021 (c to mean IQ r=.19, five samples), but strongly in Bates and Gupta 2017 (group-IQ almost the same as average IQ; Study 1 beta .76). The camps differ by lab: Woolley-affiliated r=.10, independent r=.32.
schema_part: G (do not build on c); memory
agent_test: Compare group factor against mean and max single-agent score at equal tokens; the LLM result (mean ability 37% importance) leans toward the Bates side.

claim: Social sensitivity (RME) and proportion female as predictors of c are not robust: Engel 2014 r=.53 and .55 (68 groups) but Bates and Gupta found no effect on the latent factor in joint SEM of Studies 2 and 3, and a 2025 dyad study found social sensitivity beta fell from .39 to .22 once intelligence and confidence entered.
agent_test: No direct agent analogue; do not add a social-sensitivity module on this evidence.

claim: Turn-taking evenness as a cause of higher c was not supported in Bates and Gupta (all three studies) or the 2025 dyad study (beta=.08 ns), though Woolley and Engel reported it.
agent_test: Do not hard-code equal speaking turns in debate protocols without a direct test.

claim: The factor structure is not universal: Barlow and Dennis 2016 (86 groups, 4 tasks) found mean inter-task r=-0.05 and no single factor; Credé and Howardson 2017 reanalysis of six samples concluded the data do not support one general factor across wide task sets (Rowe's coding finds support in 5 of 6). The readings of the same data differ. A 2019 meta-analysis of 745 teams (Graf, Gimpel, Barlow) found a one-factor CFA fits badly (CFI .73, RMSEA .10) with first factor 17%.
agent_test: State which tasks are in the battery; a factor from 4 similar tasks says little.

claim: Dependence on the research group: only 7 of 19 samples in Rowe 2021 were independent of Woolley and co-authors; Woolley-affiliated c-to-IQ r=.10 vs independent r=.32. Nesting, low effort and task choice are contested (Credé); the Woolley, Kim, Malone 2018 rebuttal was not read.
agent_test: None direct. Treat human c numbers as pooled across non-independent labs.

claim: About 80% of studies in Rowe 2021 lacked power to detect the main correlations (84 to 782 groups needed for r=.30 to .10), and heterogeneity of c to criterion is high (I2 86.5%).
agent_test: Use enough items and seeds; report CIs on every agent comparison.

claim: Two-factor and three-factor solutions fit some human data better than one: Graf 2019 (745 teams, one-factor CFI .73, first factor 17%, parallel analysis says 3 factors), Rowe 2024 (N=85, two-factor), Kommol, Riedl, Woolley 2025 preprint (22 studies, 1,356 groups, hierarchical three-factor memory/attention/reasoning), and a 2025 dyad study.
agent_test: Fit one- and two-factor models to agent task scores before assuming one.

claim: In human groups, collaboration process variables (skill congruence, strategy, effort) rank above individual skill in Riedl 2021 random forests overall, but individual skill dominates for some tasks (Sudoku over 51% individual; Unscramble 55% process). Task type moderates what matters.
agent_test: Test whether adding a process step helps only on tasks where coordination is needed.

claim: LLM groups show a stronger single factor than human groups: Zhou 2026, 108 groups, 8 LLMs, 5 tasks, mean r=.55 (human .28), first factor 66.3%, second 18.7%, CFA CFI .967. One framework (debate), groups under 10 agents, and shared single-model ability limit this.
agent_test: Replicate with another protocol (not debate) and check how much of the factor is just single-model ability.

claim: In LLM groups, skill congruence (over 50%) and mean member ability (37%) predict the factor; group size, max ability and effort each under 5%. A cheaper centralized group had ACI 9.7% higher than a group with 75% higher cost and stronger LLMs (the dearer group had the lower ACI; evidence a24 states this the wrong way round).
agent_test: Compare central-hub vs fully connected topologies at equal token budget.

claim: Plugging the LLM factor into multi-agent optimisers (GPTSwarm, G-Designer) gave 1.1% to 12.3% gains on unseen tasks, average 4.6%, with leave-one-task-out tests. Table 1 reports one run per cell with no seeds or CIs, so gain versus noise is unknown.
agent_test: Small gain, one team, no cost control reported; test at equal tokens before use.

claim: A general factor across LLMs (not groups) exists: Ilic and Gignac 2024, 591 LLMs, 12 tests, general factor 65.6%, mean loading .81, CFI .984, RMSEA .089, parameter count correlates with it with diminishing returns. This is model-level g, not group c.
agent_test: Pooled model comparison confounds scale; use within-model scaffold comparisons.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Persona or theory-of-mind prompts did not change success in a no-communication guessing game (GPT-4.1, N=10, 200 runs per condition, no significant difference), while each extra agent cut odds of success by about 8% (OR .92) and +1 temperature raised them by about 50% (OR 1.5; 7,150 runs).
agent_test: Do not assume a social-framing prompt alone helps; test at equal tokens.

claim: Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat single-agent baselines: Smit 2024 (GPT-3.5, MedQA: single .60, Society of Mind .64, Multi-Persona .58; GPQA single .33 vs SoM .27) and Zhang 2025 (GPT-4o-mini SoM below CoT on all nine datasets; CoT mean 72.5 vs heterogeneous SoM 76.7). Equal-budget work since: Wang 2024 (SC beats MAD, MAD falls with more budget, answer entropy shrinks), Tran and Kiela 2026 (single agent matches or beats 5 multi-agent designs at equal thinking tokens; avg 0.427 vs debate 0.420 at 100 tokens), Hu 2026 (each protocol wins somewhere; oracle routing +14 pp but cheap routing recovers 11 to 19%), Bertalanic 2026 (debate 2.1 to 3.4 times the tokens for equal or lower accuracy). Counter: Wunderlich 2026 finds debate +1.3 and MoA +2.7 points over SC at equal FLOPs on MMLU-Pro and BBH.
agent_test: Run self-consistency and debate at equal tokens; heterogeneous models were the one setting that helped.

claim: LLM groups are poor at pooling hidden information: HiddenBench, GPT-4.1 hidden-profile post-discussion accuracy .233 vs full-information .733 (30 sessions, p<.001); humans .385 vs .604 (8 sessions); best model Gemini-2.5-Pro .671; only an extreme conflict prompt helped modestly. HiddenBench v3 ablations (GPT-4.1, 3 tasks): Reveal-All (each agent states all private facts in round 1) gives 0.967 vs 0.233; a passive secretary 0.100; one adversarial agent 0.492; telling agents to share everything 0.467; groups of 7 gain +0.006 vs +0.348 at 3.
agent_test: Test whether forcing each sub-agent to state private facts raises hidden-profile accuracy.

claim: No randomised intervention that raised c itself AND transferred to held-out tasks was found. Randomised work exists but is mixed: Woolley 2022 (146 teams, hierarchy manipulation changed speech, CI effect conditional on gender mix), McDonald 2026 (live feedback on effort/skills/coordination did not help, effort-only feedback hurt), Gupta 2024 nudges (168 groups, one skill-discussion nudge helped, others hurt; search summary only). The practical lesson is task-skill matching, so c is a poor design target for our agent.
agent_test: Score design choices by held-out task performance at equal tokens, not by a c-like composite.

claim: Gap 2 is still open. Zhou 2026 computes an individual g for each of 8 LLMs and uses the mean as a predictor (37% importance), but does not report a factor analysis of single-agent scores versus the group factor on the same tasks, and reports no repeated runs. The 66.3% LLM group factor therefore cannot be separated from shared single-model ability.
agent_test: Run single-agent and group versions on the same battery at equal tokens and compare factor shares.

claim: Hidden-profile failure in LLM groups is a disclosure failure, not a reasoning failure: when every agent is forced to state its private facts in round one, GPT-4.1 accuracy goes from 0.233 to 0.967; a summary-only secretary agent gives 0.100; prompts to share all information give 0.467.
agent_test: Add a private-fact listing step to sub-agent contexts and compare with a passive summariser at equal tokens; the oracle Reveal-All number is an upper bound.

claim: Debate failure modes at small scale are documented: sycophantic conformity (modal adoption up to 85.5%), contextual fragility (up to 70.0% of correct answers destabilised) and consensus collapse (oracle gap up to 32.3 pp), at 2.1 to 3.4 times the tokens of self-correction; answer entropy falls each debate round.
agent_test: Track answer entropy per round in any debate operator and stop when it collapses.

claim: Whether to use debate cannot be predicted cheaply: an oracle protocol router gains about +14 pp over the best fixed protocol, but vote entropy captures only 11 to 19% and 66% of debate-helpful cases are unanimous-but-wrong.
agent_test: Do not gate debate on self-agreement alone.

claim: Gaps 3, 7, 9 stay open after this pass: no first-factor values per sample from Credé and Howardson, no fit indices from Kommol, Riedl, Woolley 2025, and no new independent test of the c-to-IQ difference (r=.32 independent vs .10 Woolley-lab). The 2018 Woolley reply was seen only as a search summary.
agent_test: None; keep human c numbers marked as lab-dependent.
